Alone at Silvermount, Emmett Rusk whispered “Bluebell” and dropped the glass snow globe. It hit the floor and shattered, the tiny flakes scattering as his body slumped against the endless mirrors.

A newsreel obituary recited his public life: the failed governor’s campaign, the Clarion he had built, the opera house he had financed. It closed without explaining his last word.

A reporter named Nash was sent to find out what “Bluebell” meant. He found Nora in a seaside nightclub, drunk, and she turned him away.

Long before any of that, in a mining boarding house out west, Emmett’s mother signed her son over to the banker Barrow after a defaulted lodger’s mine deed made the family rich. The boy drove his sled into Barrow’s stomach—a desperate, childish blow—and was taken east anyway.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett took control of the fortune. He told Barrow that of all his holdings, he wanted to run a failing city newspaper, the Clarion. He moved into its offices, installed his manager Marsh and his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Then he hired away the entire staff of the rival paper and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line.

He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor’s niece. Their marriage cooled into silence behind separate newspapers at breakfast. He met a shopgirl named Nora Kell on the street with mud on his coat; he started visiting her rooms in secret.

Mid-campaign for governor, the party boss Halloran brought Adele to Nora’s rooms and threatened exposure. Emmett refused to withdraw. He lost the election. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city. The marriage collapsed.

Nora’s debut was a humiliation—her voice cracked on the high notes. Devlin, drunk, began a savage review. Emmett finished it, printed it, and fired him. Then he married Nora and forced her into an opera career for which she had no voice.

She swallowed poison rather than sing again. Emmett finally let her stop.

He shut her away in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles in the vast empty hall. After a joyless beach picnic and a quarrel, she packed and left him. He wrecked her bedroom, found a glass snow globe, murmured “Bluebell,” and carried it past the endless mirrors.

Nash read Barrow’s memoir. He interviewed Marsh, Devlin, a drunken Nora, and the butler Colm. He concluded that no single word explains a life.

Outside the boiler room, workmen shoveled a sled marked *Bluebell* into the furnace.

Over breakfast, the crew argued about a pop song on the diner radio. Cal insisted it was about a girl, Bram said it was about a stolen car, and Mr. Ash just shrugged. When the waitress came by, Mr. Birch left a quarter. Cal called it an insult. Bram said she earned it. The argument died with the coffee.

Later, in the warehouse, Mr. Ash cradled Mr. Elm. Elm was screaming, a wet gurgle from the bullet in his stomach. “You’re not dying,” Ash swore, pressing a rag to the wound. Elm’s face was gray, but his eyes stayed open.

Mr. Birch arrived, still fuming. “That job was a setup. There’s an informer inside.” He hid the diamonds behind a loose brick near the door, then stood guard.

Bram handed out aliases from a list of trees. “Mr. Ash. Mr. Birch. Mr. Cedar. Mr. Elm.” Birch scowled. “I’m not a birch. That’s a woman’s name.” No one laughed.

Mr. Cedar strolled in last, whistling. He opened the boot of his car and hauled out a bound patrolman. Doyle. He dropped him on the concrete.

Ren Vasco walked through the door an hour later, still smelling of prison. He shook hands with Bram and Cal. “You owe me,” he said. Bram nodded. “You’ll get your cut.”

Left alone with Doyle, Mr. Cedar turned on the radio. An oldie played. He danced a few steps, then knelt, sliced off the man’s ear with a straight razor, and doused him in petrol. Doyle whimpered.

From the floor, Mr. Elm raised his pistol and shot Mr. Cedar twice in the chest. Cedar fell. Elm turned to Doyle. “I’m a cop. Police are waiting outside for Bram.”

But that was a future that had already been rehearsed. Earlier, in a safe house, undercover officer Danny Roarke had sat across from his handler Pruitt. “Tell it like it’s a memory,” Pruitt said. Danny repeated the anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet until the lie felt true. Then he performed it for Bram, for Cal, for Mr. Ash. They believed him. They called him Mr. Elm.

The robbery had collapsed within a minute. Mr. Ash shot his way clear from the getaway car, Elm beside him. They fled on foot. Elm hijacked a sedan, but the driver shot him in the stomach. Elm shot the driver dead. Ash took the wheel, drove Elm to the warehouse, screaming all the way.

Now Cal returned from the street. He listened to Elm’s account of Cedar, then walked over to Doyle and shot him in the head.

Bram arrived last. He looked at the bodies, at the blood, at Elm on the floor. “He’s the informer,” Bram said. Mr. Ash refused to believe it. He turned his gun on Bram.

The three-way standoff lasted three seconds. Bram fired at Ash, Cal fired at Ash, Ash fired at Bram. Bram fell. Cal fell. Ash fell. Only Ash and Elm were still breathing.

Elm confessed then, his voice wet. “I’m a police officer.” Ash raised his gun and shot him. The police stormed the warehouse. A dozen guns cut Ash down.

The diamonds stayed hidden behind the loose brick. No one ever found them.

The shot echoed in the derelict building. Roy Mercer’s body crumpled, and Martin Kray lowered the gun, his hand steady. He photographed the corpse, the flash bleaching the blood. He didn’t know why he was here, only that the license plate on his thigh—inked hours ago, the sixth fact—had told him this was the man. The initials R.M. matched a scarred memory from a bathroom attack he couldn’t fully hold.

Later, in a motel room he didn’t remember checking into, Martin held a phone to his ear and told the anonymous caller about a case. Elias Prine had claimed memory loss after his diabetic wife died. Martin had ruled it psychosomatic, denied the claim. He’d been sure the man was faking. He didn’t recall the caller’s name, only that he needed to listen.

Corinne, the bartender with the dead man’s clothes on her eyes, slid him a paper. “Ran the plate through a friend at the registry. Roy Mercer.” She handed him a record. Martin stared at the name. The same initials from the bathroom. The same ones that had sent him into that building.

He remembered the interview: Elias Prine, hollow-eyed, insisting he couldn’t recall giving his wife injections. Martin had been certain it was a lie. He’d written “psychosomatic” in the file.

Now he drove a man named Vance out of town at gunpoint, having beaten him in a motel bathroom. Vance was a name Corinne had given him, her face bruised. She’d hidden every pen in her house, goaded him into hitting her, then blamed Vance. He’d believed her.

But earlier, long before, there had been another woman—Elias’s wife. She tested her husband by asking for injection after injection, and he, unable to remember, gave her the lethal overdose. Martin had denied that claim.

Corinne had served him a beer the staff had spat in. She recognized the dead man’s suit—Gil Marsh’s suit—and the car. She knew something.

The attack in the bathroom: intruders, his wife screaming, a blade, a bullet, his skull cracking against tile. He killed one man, but the other fled. Martin woke with a brain that couldn’t form new memories. He built a system: instant photographs, annotated notes, tattoos on his own skin. The initials R.M. were the first fact.

He burned his wife’s hairbrush and books in a field, trying to grieve a loss that disappeared every minute. The ashes settled like snow.

The caller had fed him a name and location: Gil Marsh, a drug dealer in a basement. Martin went, beat him, strangled him, and photographed the body. As Gil died, he whispered “Elias.” Martin didn’t understand. He changed into Gil’s suit, took his sports car.

Then Roy arrived—the plainclothes officer who, a year ago, helped Martin find and kill the real attacker from the bathroom. Roy had lured the man to a warehouse; Martin shot him, then forgot within minutes. Now Roy said, “Gil was innocent. You already avenged your wife. And you are Elias Prine.”

Martin didn’t believe him. He burned the photographs of Gil. On Roy’s picture he wrote “he is lying to you.” And when Roy drove away, Martin copied down his license plate—his next target.

At the tattoo parlor, he had the plate inked on his thigh. Sixth fact. Then he lured Roy to the derelict building. For all he knew, this was justice.

The gun was still warm. He didn’t remember why any of this started, but the scars on his skin told the only story he owned.

Rex beats me down a stairwell in one of the towers. My ribs crack, my vision blurs, and I taste blood. I pull the gun from my waistband, press the barrel against my palate, and squeeze the trigger. The bullet exits through my cheek, shattering teeth. Rex falls with me. We are the same.

Before all this, I was an insomniac product-recall investigator. The only thing that let me sleep was crying at support groups for diseases I did not have. I would sit in the back of a room full of strangers, let the grief wash over me, and sob until exhaustion took me.

Then Ada Vey started attending the same groups. She was obvious faking—her tears never reached her eyes, her stories were too polished. Her presence destroyed my release. I couldn't cry anymore; I just watched her and felt rage.

On a business flight I met soap salesman Rex Marrow. He had a salesman’s grin and a pocket full of cards. I took one, not knowing why.

My flat and all my catalogue furniture were destroyed in an explosion. I had nothing. I called Rex. He took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district. The walls were damp, the windows boarded, but it was shelter.

Outside a bar, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could. I did. Then he hit me. We beat each other bloody in the car park, fists cracking bone, until we collapsed laughing.

What started as two men brawling hardened into a weekly basement club. We made rules: no weapons, no stopping until one yields. More men came. The club grew.

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the derelict house. They began a loud affair I could not stand. I heard them through the thin walls every night.

Rex had a side business: he rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. The soap smelled of roses and hospital.

One night, Rex burned my hand with lye. He held it there, refusing to let me retreat into meditation. I screamed. He said, “Feel it.”

I blackmailed my employer into paying me to stay away, using my own beaten face as evidence. They paid. I had money, but I stayed.

Rex turned the club into an organisation he called Havoc. He filled the house with shaven recruits who took orders and vandalised corporate property. I watched from the shadows.

Then Rex steered the car into oncoming traffic. He let it roll, then opened the door and disappeared. I was alone.

A member of Havoc named Ogden was shot dead on an operation. I started trying to shut the whole thing down. I travelled city to city, but I found identical clubs everywhere. Men greeted me as Rex Marrow.

I worked it out: Rex and I are the same person. He has been acting while I sleep. My insomnia was his waking.

Ada confirmed it. She had been sleeping with me, not with a separate man. She said, “You don’t remember, do you?”

I discovered that Havoc had mined the towers of the debt-record companies. I tried to defuse the charges. I climbed the stairwell, sweating, cutting wires.

Rex beat me down that stairwell. Now I lie here, blood pooling, the gun smoking in my hand. We are one.

Ada is delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. She finds me on the landing, face half-gone, and takes my hand. We hold each other at the window as the buildings come down. The explosions are beautiful. I am awake.

Over eggs and coffee, two small-time robbers named Eddie and Lou decided on the spot to hold up the diner they were sitting in. They had nothing but a zip-tie and a steak knife, but the register was fat and the morning crowd was soft.

Across the city, Rollo and Marcus cruised in a borrowed sedan, debating whether they called hamburgers “burgers” in France or “steak haché” and if the Dutch really let you smoke weed on a park bench. Rollo argued for pragmatism; Marcus cited scripture.

Outside a flat in a tired building, they waited. “You think a foot massage is worth killing a man for?” Rollo asked. Marcus didn’t answer. He recited a passage from Psalms, and they kicked the door in. Tobin was on the couch, a briefcase at his feet. They shot him twice for double-crossing Otis, recovered the case, and left.

They delivered it to Otis at his bar. Otis was paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth. Denny pocketed the cash and nodded.

That night, Rollo bought heroin from his dealer Kip, shot up in the bathroom, then took Otis’s wife Nadia to a themed diner shaped like a spaceship. They won the dance contest—a plastic trophy and a free milkshake. Later, at Kip’s place, Nadia snorted Rollo’s stash and stopped breathing. Kip jabbed an adrenaline shot into her heart on the living-room floor. She gasped back.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war had handed a young boy—Denny—a gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity. The boy had worn it ever since.

In the ring, Denny double-crossed Otis. He won the fight, killed his opponent with a brutal right hook, and escaped in a taxi. Hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, he reached for his pocket and found nothing. She had left his father’s watch behind in his flat. Denny went back.

The flat was empty except for Rollo, who was cooking eggs in the kitchen. A submachine gun sat on the counter. Denny picked it up and shot Rollo dead. He grabbed the watch from the nightstand and ran.

In the street, Denny’s taxi collided with Otis’s car. Both men were taken prisoner by a crew that ran a pawnshop. They were locked in the basement. One of the captors started raping Otis. Denny broke his zip-ties, grabbed a sword from the shop wall, and cut the man down. Otis, bleeding and humiliated, declared them square—on condition Denny left town. Denny collected Marielle from the motel and rode out of the city on a motorcycle stolen from the pawnshop.

Back in the flat, after Rollo and Marcus had shot Tobin, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them. Every shot missed. Marcus called it divine intervention. In the car afterwards, Rollo’s gun went off and blew the head off their passenger Del. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren’s house, where a fixer directed the cleanup and gave them fresh clothes.

Over breakfast in a coffee shop—the same one Eddie and Lou had tried to rob—Marcus sat with the briefcase. A nervous kid with a steak knife tried to hold up the place. Marcus talked him down, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out. He finished his coffee alone.

Detective Isaiah Reece stood over the body by the roadside, the rain washing the blood from his brother’s face. Kwame’s eyes were open, fixed on nothing. Reece’s mother would later ask why he never went looking, but right now he could only stare at the hole in Kwame’s chest.

Nadir and his daughter Sahar bought a handgun from a dealer who mimicked his accent. “You speak good English for a shopkeeper,” the man said, grinning. Nadir counted out the cash, his hands steady.

Trey and Kwame carjacked the prosecutor Halstead’s car outside a restaurant. They took his wallet, his phone, and left him on the sidewalk.

Mateo changed the Halsteads’ locks while Paula shouted from the living room, “You’re going to sell my keys to your gang, aren’t you?” Mateo said nothing, finished the job, and left.

Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts. He made Renee step out, groped her in front of her husband Clay, then let them go with a warning. Voss watched from the patrol car, jaw tight.

Tobias skipped work on an impulse he couldn’t account for, took the train to the coast, and found Ivy on the frozen sand. She was tracing circles with her boot, her breath a ghost in the cold air. “You came,” she said, and he nodded, not knowing why.

They drove back to the city together, and she invited him up to her flat. The walls were bare except for a single photograph—a beach house at dusk. He stared at it. “I feel like I’ve been there,” he said. She smiled, but her eyes were distant.

A week later, he walked into the bookshop where she worked. She looked through him. “Can I help you?” she asked, polite and blank. A young man named Peck leaned over the counter, and she laughed at something he said. Tobias’s chest caved.

She had hired a memory-erasure clinic to remove every trace of him. Nina and Grady showed him the form letter. He went straight to Dr. Hallam and demanded the same procedure. “Box up everything connected to her,” Hallam said. “We’ll map the memories.”

Tobias spent an evening boxing objects: a seashell, a scarf, a ticket stub from the drive-in. The technicians Dell and Peck arrived at his flat to run the overnight erasure. While Tobias lay on the bed, Peck pocketed a small shell—to use on Ivy later, he whispered to Dell.

Inside his own head, Tobias watched the most recent and ugliest memories dissolve: Ivy coming home drunk, the dent in his car door, the fight that ended with her walking out. The recriminations over her drinking and his withholding scattered like ash.

But then something went wrong. Dell and the receptionist Rosa got high on Tobias’s bed, laughing, and lost track of the procedure. The map went off the rails. In the chaos, Tobias changed his mind. He tried to smuggle Ivy into memories she was never part of—a childhood birthday, a rainy afternoon alone. He reached for the early days: the ice on the frozen river where they’d skated, the noodle house where she’d stolen his chopsticks, the drive-in where she’d fallen asleep on his shoulder. Two years of falling in love.

Dr. Hallam arrived to re-map the erasure. Rosa kissed him in the hallway. His wife appeared, furious, and revealed that Rosa’s own affair with Hallam had been erased months ago. The clinic was a house of cards.

In the last surviving memory, Tobias stood with Ivy in the empty house on the shore—the night they’d broken in after the beach party. She was a stranger then. “If we ever lose each other,” she said, “meet me here.” He promised.

The erasure completed. Tobias woke the next morning with no memory that Ivy ever existed. He got out of bed, confused by the boxes, the strange shell in his pocket.

Rosa quit the clinic that day. She mailed the files and session tapes back to every patient on the books. A package arrived at Tobias’s flat. He opened it, found a cassette, and pressed play.

Ivy’s voice filled the room, raw and familiar: “You never listened. You always held back.” Then his own voice, brittle: “You drank until you were someone else.” The tape tore them apart. Then silence. Then the click of a door.

She ran. Then the sound of footsteps returning. A long breath. “We could try again,” she whispered.

Tobias didn’t know her. But he felt the weight of that empty house, the frozen sand, the photograph on her wall. He took the train to the coast again, not knowing why. She was there, waiting on the beach. “You came,” she said. And he nodded, as if he had always known.

In a bar two years afterward, Odile told Wilder her marriage was over. She had spent the previous night confessing everything to her husband—the rented rooms, the afternoons, the whole long deception. Wilder said nothing at first, just watched the ice melt in his glass.

“He published a writer of yours,” Odile let slip. “Someone you both quietly detest.”

Wilder’s face changed. He rang Emlyn that same evening, in a state. Emlyn came to his house before the night was out.

“I have known for four years,” Emlyn said. “My wife told me on the trip abroad. And I never thought much of your letters either.”

Before that, Wilder and Odile had decided the rented rooms had become a chore. They split the crockery and surrendered the lease, dividing plates and cups as if dividing memory itself. And before that, there was a dinner at the married couple’s house—the two men discussing racquet games and schoolboy sport until Odile had no part in the talk at all. She sat silent, watching them volley words across the table.

Before that, in a hotel abroad, Emlyn had asked about a letter held for her at the desk, addressed in a hand he recognized. She confessed. He remarked that he had always been fonder of his friend than of his wife. The words hung in the hotel room like smoke.

Odile went back to the rented rooms and said nothing whatever about the trip. The afternoon passed exactly as the others had—the same light through the same curtains, the same quiet. And before that, Emlyn had drunk through a long restaurant lunch with Wilder, baiting him about contemporary fiction, never once mentioning what he had learned. He smiled and poured more wine.

Still earlier, Wilder and Odile had rented rooms in a quiet district and filled them with linen and plates, giving the affair a household of its own. They chose the sheets together, the cups, the salt cellar. Then Odile said she was carrying her husband’s child, and they decided the rented rooms would go on exactly as before. Nothing would change.

Before all that, during a party at the house of his closest friend, a book agent named Wilder led Odile to an upstairs room and told her how lovely she was while the other guests drank downstairs. The music drifted up the stairs. She had not said no. She had not said anything at all.

Solly Two Coats and his crew, dressed as devout pilgrims, walked out of a diamond house in a northern port with a stone the size of a fist. Word of the heist had yet to travel, but across the sea, his cousin Marv was already sending orders: bring it straight over.

Meanwhile, in the city, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. But the bare-knuckle fighter Finn knocked Sam out cold over the deal, leaving Halloway without a man for the fixed bout promised to gang boss Coldstone. With no other option, Halloway put Finn in the fight instead and swore to Coldstone that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly had other concerns. Grigor the Nail told him about a bookmaker’s in the city, perfect for placing a bet on the fight—and simultaneously tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob him there. Solly landed, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch, and headed for the bookmaker’s, case in hand.

But Finn knocked his opponent out cold in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway with a beating. Meanwhile, Ike, Benno, and Tulley bungled the robbery: they took Solly’s arm—literally, shot it off—and his case, then were chased off by Grigor. Marv flew in to find Solly gone and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to find him.

Grigor took Solly, cut off his other arm to get the case open, and found the stone wasn’t inside. Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs and told Halloway and Digby what would happen if the second fight went wrong. Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took both them and the stone.

Halloway and Digby told Finn to go down in the fourth. To ensure compliance, Coldstone’s men burned Finn’s mother to death in her caravan. Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car with Ike and Benno inside; in the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Only Tulley got away—with the dog that had swallowed the diamond.

In the second fight, Finn knocked his opponent out again in the fourth round. The travellers in the crowd massacred Coldstone’s men. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone and shot him dead. By morning, the travellers had vanished.

The dog was handed in at a pet shop, coughed up the diamond, and Halloway and Digby ended up holding it. They stared at the stone, silent, as the last threads of the scheme unraveled in their hands.

Lena’s voice was ice as she said it: “Kill him.” Aaron bought the gun that afternoon, a cheap revolver from a pawnshop, and tracked Wes Tarrow to a motel on the edge of town.

Wes Tarrow had once been an ex-con, newly born again. He held down a job at a warehouse and coached boys’ baseball on weekends. His wife Nita dreaded his fanaticism and his temper—the way his eyes went flat when he talked about sin and redemption.

Lena Ward had been a recovered addict. She lived a settled life with her husband Doug and their two young daughters in a house with a white fence and a garden she tended every morning.

Mathematician Aaron Vale sat in a doctor’s office and heard the words: his failing heart would kill him within weeks unless a donor was found. He nodded, thinking of equations and probability, and then called his estranged wife Della.

Lena went back to cocaine. She began methodically destroying herself, snorting lines in the bathroom while the girls’ crayon drawings curled on the fridge.

Wes’s pickup hit Doug and both girls at a crosswalk. He slammed the brakes, saw the bodies, then drove off. He turned back after a block, saw the blood spreading, and fled again.

Della pressed Aaron to agree to be inseminated with his frozen sperm before he died. “A legacy,” she said. He signed the papers without reading them.

At the hospital, Lena was told her husband and both children were dead. She stared at the ceiling tiles and did not cry.

Wes walked into a police station and confessed to the hit-and-run. He was sentenced and sent to prison. Inside, he prayed.

Doug’s heart was transplanted into Aaron. He woke up for the first time in months, feeling the steady beat in his chest, a stranger’s rhythm.

Unable to stop thinking about whose heart was beating inside him, Aaron hired a private investigator. The report came back: the donor was Douglas Ward, killed with his daughters by a drunk driver. The widow was Lena.

Released early on good behavior, Wes walked out on Nita and on his faith. He took a job at a motel far from home, cleaning rooms and drinking alone.

Aaron followed Lena. He engineered a meeting at a swimming pool, pretended to struggle in the water. She pulled him out, and they began an affair. He told her his name was Alex.

Aaron left Della and told her he did not want the child she was trying to conceive. “I’m sorry,” he said. She hung up.

At the motel, Aaron raised the gun. He aimed at Wes’s chest, but his hand trembled. He could not go through with it. He fired wide, hitting Wes in the shoulder, and told him to run.

That night, Aaron admitted to Lena that he was carrying her husband’s heart. She threw him out of the apartment, then ran after him and took him back, sobbing against his chest.

Wes followed the pair back to their motel room. He stood in the doorway, blood seeping through his bandage, and asked Aaron to finish the job. “I deserve it,” he said. Aaron turned the gun on himself instead.

Lena and Wes got the dying Aaron to a hospital. The transplanted heart failed on the operating table. Wes went home to his family—Nita had taken him back—and Lena, pregnant with Aaron’s child, went home alone.

He was conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. The ship’s hold stank of vomit and rust, and he prayed to a god he barely believed in, mouthing the words the chaplain had taught him. Then the aliens came. They took him from the deck in a beam of cold light, and he found himself in a zoo on their planet, standing beside a film actress whose name he had once seen on a marquee. The enclosure was a perfect replica of a small-town street, but the sky was wrong—too many stars, too bright. The aliens spoke inside his skull, explaining that every moment exists at once, that free will was an idea peculiar to his own planet. He tried to understand, but the actress only wept.

Before the aliens, he had been a boy born in a small industrial town, weak and peculiar, with limbs that seemed too long for his body. He had grown into a child who flinched at loud noises and preferred the company of stray cats. His father, a man of gruff practicality, threw him into the deep end of a pool to teach him to swim. He sank to the bottom, bubbles streaming from his nose, and lay there until a lifeguard pulled him out. He never learned to swim.

After the zoo, he was sent on to a great city and housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir. The hooks still swung from the ceiling, and the floor was slick with old blood. He shared a corner with a man who coughed black phlegm. Then he came home, collapsed, and was hospitalised. In the ward, another patient introduced him to a hack science fiction writer—a gaunt man with yellowed fingers who talked about parallel dimensions. The writer gave him a stack of magazines, and he read them under the sheets with a penlight.

The aliens had said time was a lake, not a river. He thought of that when the city was destroyed by fire in one night. The prisoners in the meat locker came up to find it gone—the abattoir, the streets, the skyline—all replaced by a smoking plain. They were made to dig bodies out of the cellars until one of the diggers died of the dry heaves, retching nothing. He dug until his hands bled.

His daughter decided he was senile and took his affairs out of his hands. She had always been practical, like her mother. Her mother had died of exhaust fumes driving to the hospital after an air crash in the mountains. He had survived that crash, walking away with a broken collarbone while the plane burned. His wife had started the car in the garage to get warm, forgetting the door was closed. He remembered the smell of the garage, the way the cat had yowled.

He was lost behind the lines with a scout who beat him for wanting to be left to die. The scout’s fists were hard, and he took the blows without crying. They were captured, and the scout died of gangrene on the prison train, blaming him with his last breath. A fellow prisoner later promised to have him killed one day on the dead scout’s account. He married the daughter of the man who owned the optometry school and became rich. He sat in a house with a swimming pool he never used, and his wife smiled at parties.

He went on a radio talk show and tried to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. The host cut him off, and the callers laughed. He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. They were polite, sharing their cigarettes. He was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he had always known he would be. The beam came from the sky, and he fell without a sound. The crowd scattered. The scout’s ghost, if there was one, would have to wait.

He sank to the bottom, bubbles streaming from his nose, and lay there until a lifeguard pulled him out. He never learned to swim.

He shared a corner with a man who coughed black phlegm. Then he came home, collapsed, and was hospitalised. In the ward, another patient introduced him to a hack science fiction writer—a gaunt man with yellowed fingers who talked about parallel dimensions. The writer gave him a stack of magazines, and he read them under the sheets with a penlight.

The aliens had said time was a lake, not a river. He thought of that when the city was destroyed by fire in one night. He was held in a camp beside enemy officers who had been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. They were polite, sharing their cigarettes. He was shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd, exactly as he had always known he would be. The beam came from the sky, and he fell without a sound. The crowd scattered. The scout’s ghost, if there was one, would have to wait.

Ruben ran a red light at speed and ploughed into Celine’s car. The crash tore through the intersection, scattering glass and metal. But to understand how he came to that moment, you have to go back to the cramped house he shared with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and their baby. The walls were thin, the air thick with resentment.

Nestor robbed a pharmacy by night and came home to beat Alma. Ruben watched, then began pressing her to run away with him. She hesitated, trapped by the child and fear. Meanwhile, Ruben discovered that Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight. He started entering the dog in local fights, winning steadily, the money piling up in a hidden stash.

Ruben paid two thugs to beat Nestor. But Nestor responded by taking Alma, the baby, and Ruben’s hidden savings, vanishing without a trace. In the last fight, the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring. Ruben stabbed Chaco and fled with his friend Pipo, the dog left bleeding. Later, Nestor was shot dead robbing a bank. At the funeral, Alma stood by the grave, and Ruben made his last offer for her to leave with him. She refused, turning away.

Meanwhile, model Celine Vaz had her own story. Her lover Hector walked out on his wife and daughters and moved her into a new flat that faced her own billboard. Celine woke in a hospital bed with her leg pinned together by surgeons; her lapdog Chispa was lost somewhere in the flat. While she lay helpless, Chispa fell through a hole in the floorboards. Hector tore up the floor searching, but Celine’s leg turned gangrenous. The leg was amputated. The billboard carrying her image was taken down.

Elsewhere, the businessman Elian hired a man named Cardo to murder his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Cardo, a former guerrilla turned contract killer, first watched from a distance as his estranged wife was buried, then followed his grown daughter Perla home. Days later, Cardo came upon the wreckage at the junction where Ruben had crashed. He dragged the bleeding Tigre out of the wreck, the dog still alive despite its wounds. Cardo nursed Tigre back to health among his own pack of strays.

But Tigre killed every other dog in Cardo’s yard while he was out. Cardo put a gun to the dog’s head and could not fire. Instead, he abducted Sergio but chained him up in his lair instead of killing him. Then Cardo brought Elian face to face with his brother, left a loaded pistol between them, and walked out having taken money from both. Finally, he broke into Perla’s flat, left a long confession on her answering machine, and took her photograph. Shaved and in clean clothes, Cardo left his money for Perla and walked out into the wasteland with Tigre at his side.

In a flat overlooking the street, an old man pressed his palm against the cool glass and spoke to the younger one beside him. “Nothing survives time,” he said. “Not the violence, not the memory, not the ones we try to save.” Below, the flashing lights of police cars bled red across the wet asphalt. Two officers were handcuffing a man with a broken arm—Cort—and another, Jonah, whose knuckles were still raw and bleeding. They were carried out of the club called the Pit, their heads bowed, while a small crowd gathered and dispersed.

Minutes earlier, inside that club, Jonah had raised a fire extinguisher and brought it down on a man’s face. The man had already been seized by Cort—the wrong man, a stranger with no name. Cort had grabbed him by the collar, demanding answers, and the man had twisted free, snapping Cort’s arm at the elbow with a sickening crack. Jonah had seen it happen, had seen the real target—the Adder—watching from a few feet away, leaning against the bar with a cold smile. So Jonah had taken the extinguisher and beaten the wrong man’s face until it was pulp, while the Adder watched and did nothing.

Before that, two men had approached Cort and Jonah on the street outside the party. They had offered to sell the name of the rapist for a price. “The Adder,” one had said. “He works out of the Pit.” And they had steered the two men toward the club, their hands in their pockets, their eyes flat.

Before that, Cort and Jonah had come stumbling out of the party to find Lise being loaded into an ambulance. Her face was a mask of blood, her dress torn, her eyes closed. A paramedic was shouting. Cort had tried to reach her, but someone held him back. Jonah had stood frozen, watching the doors close.

Before that, in the pedestrian underpass, the Adder had raped Lise. He had beaten her head against the concrete wall until her hair was wet and dark. A passer-by had glimpsed them, had seen the pimp’s fist rise and fall, and had backed away, turned, and walked faster.

Before that, Lise had taken the underpass instead of crossing the busy road. She had walked in on the pimp known as the Adder beating a transsexual woman. The woman was on her knees, her lip split, her wig askew. Lise had stopped, and the Adder had looked up.

Before that, at the party, Cort had gotten steadily drunk and high. He had started pursuing other women, his hands wandering, his laugh too loud. Lise had watched from the corner, disgusted, and then she had left on her own, pulling her jacket tight.

Before that, Lise, Cort, and Jonah had ridden the underground train to the party. They had argued cheerfully about sex and about Cort’s drinking. Jonah had laughed and said Cort was a lightweight. Lise had rolled her eyes but smiled. The train had rattled through the dark tunnels, and she had felt something flutter in her chest.

Before that, Lise had lain in bed with Cort, describing a recurring dream of a red tunnel. “It’s warm and it pulls me,” she had said. Cort had teased her about her ex-boyfriend Jonah, about how she still dreamed of him. “I don’t dream of him,” she had said, but they had both laughed, and she had traced a pattern on his chest.

Later that morning, alone in the flat, Lise had taken a pregnancy test. The little window showed a plus sign. She had sat on the edge of the tub for a long time, the plastic stick cold in her hand.

And before that—or after, it didn’t matter now—she had sat in the park among the sprinklers and playing children. She had held a book open in her lap, but she wasn’t reading. Her hand rested on her stomach, and the water from the sprinklers misted her skin. The children laughed and ran, and the sun was warm, and she thought of nothing at all.

Helicopters sprayed the city through the night, passing over every neighbourhood, their rotors beating against the darkness as they released pesticides against crop pests. Meanwhile, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, were getting ready for a dinner party, she adjusting her earrings while he straightened his tie. Across town, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu seethed beside her, his jealousy a slow burn that would not be extinguished. In a dimly lit club, the singer Vida performed nightly, her voice soaring over the audience, while her cellist daughter Bee played alone at home, the empty rooms echoing with her music. Officer Rowe, cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, abandoned the family dog to cover one of his lies, leaving the animal to wander the streets.

Earlier that day, a boy named Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress called Rhona on his way to school. He got up, insisted he was fine, and walked home, his parents none the wiser. The baker Otto Kemp had taken an order for a birthday cake for a boy named Charlie Rill, not knowing the accident had already occurred; he wrote the name in icing with careful loops. Later, Charlie collapsed into a coma, and his parents Grant and Elaine kept vigil at the hospital, their hopes fading with each passing hour. Meanwhile, Ike and Dot were house-sitting for the Hartigans. Dot dressed up as a beaten corpse, her face painted with bruises and blood, and Ike photographed her, the images disturbingly realistic. Stu and three friends drove out to fish and found a young woman’s body face down in the river, her hair tangled in the current. They pulled it to the bank. Nan’s ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, learned she had a new man and, in a rage, sawed her furniture to pieces, the wood splintering under his fury. Unpaid and ignored, the baker Otto started making anonymous menacing phone calls to the family, his voice a low threat on the line, saying things that made Elaine shiver. Instead of reporting the body, the men tethered it to the bank with rope and carried on fishing for two more days before telling anyone, the fish biting while the corpse floated nearby.

At the hospital, Grant’s estranged father Duff turned up and confessed an affair from decades ago, the words spilling out in a whisper that added to the family’s turmoil. Vern’s wife Iris, a party clown, was disgusted when she learned what the men had done to the body; she scrubbed her face clean of makeup, the greasepaint smearing like shame. At the dinner party, Bess admitted to a long-ago nude modelling session and an affair. Neil made a scene, shouting and upsetting the guests, glasses toppling, wine staining the tablecloth. Charlie died in hospital. Grant and Elaine went to the bakery to confront Otto, but he fed them warm bread and grieved with them, his menace dissolved into sorrow, tears mixing with flour on his apron. Bee found her mother asleep, closed the garage door, and killed herself with the car engine running, the carbon monoxide filling the space as the exhaust whispered its poison. At a picnic in the hills, Stu smashed a young woman’s head with a rock, the violence erupting without warning, blood on the grass. A tremor shook the entire city, and every death and every wreck was folded into one evening bulletin, the news anchor’s voice flat as it listed the night’s tragedies: a boy, a baker’s rage, a cellist’s silence, a woman by the river, a man with a rock, all gathered under the headline of a city that never stopped spinning.
